title: Raga Bilaval
hook: a morning raga of joy that opens with a praise-singer admitting his words are too small, and singing on

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hymn in Suhi: two brides, one who names her faults and one who says you are my wealth on a throne or with a bowl. Your line was the skilled bride. What did your one sentence do? Day one thousand ninety-six.

Calling a king sir is not a compliment. It's a downgrade. Sir is what you call the man at the next table. A king has bigger titles than that, and leaving them off is a little insult, however politely it's meant. Now turn the page of the Guru Granth Sahib to where a new raga begins. Guru Nanak opens it with exactly that problem: every title he has is too small for the One he's singing to. And he sings on anyway. Today: Raga Bilaval.
screen: `CALLING A KING SIR.` → `EVERY TITLE TOO SMALL.` → `AND SINGS ON ANYWAY.`

segments.voice: First, the place. Bilaval follows Suhi in the Granth's order. Sikh tradition, along with the wider music it grew from, links Bilaval with morning and with joy. Second, the opening line, in paraphrase: you are the Sultan; if I call you Mian, sir, what greatness is that? Mian was a respectful title in Guru Nanak's world. Set beside the One who made everything, it sounds like calling the ocean a puddle. Third, the confession that follows. Whatever you give, Master, that is what I say; I'm a fool, I can't find the words. Then the refrain, a request: give me understanding, so I can sing your praises and live in truth, by your will. Then: whatever has happened has come from you; you know everything. I can't know your limit, my Master; what cleverness do I have? And: what can I say? I speak and speak, and see that the one beyond words can't be put into words. Whatever pleases you, I say, and it's a sesame seed of your greatness. Fourth, the joy. That might sound like a defeat for a singer. A praise song that keeps admitting it can't praise. But look at what the hymn does next. It doesn't stop; it asks for understanding to keep singing. And it's set in a raga that tradition links with joy. The singer has found something too big for his vocabulary, and instead of giving up, he keeps singing, at morning, in a joyful raga. There's a freedom in it. Nobody has to find the perfect word. The perfect word doesn't exist. So the morning song can start with a small one, sir, and smile at how small it is, and still be sung gladly. That's today's line: morning joy.
screen: `BILAVAL FOLLOWS SUHI.` · `YOU ARE THE SULTAN; I SAY SIR.` · `I SPEAK, AND IT CAN'T BE SAID.` · `TOO BIG FOR WORDS, SUNG GLADLY.` · then, large: `MORNING JOY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to Bilaval, or try praising something too big. If you can, play a shabad sung in Raga Bilaval, ideally in the morning. If not, sit and let the breath settle. Now choose something larger than you: the sky this morning, the ocean, the fact that you woke up at all. Try to describe it in a few words in your head. Notice how small the words are. Don't fix them. Let it be a little funny, the way sir is funny for a sultan. Then let the words go and simply enjoy the thing itself. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once. If you don't, let a small smile be the whole response. The bell holds the time.
Raga Bilaval. The raga after Suhi, linked by tradition with morning and joy, which opens with Guru Nanak calling the Sultan sir and singing on anyway. Today's word.
Your line: morning joy. Tomorrow morning, before the day starts talking, say one small, inadequate thank-you for something too big for it, and let that be enough. Day one thousand ninety-six.

howItsDone: Shabads from the Bilaval section of the Guru Granth Sahib are sung in kirtan in Raga Bilaval, which Sikh musical tradition links with the morning and a joyful mood.

original.note: bilaval, the raga after Suhi, linked by tradition with morning and joy.

trapdoor: what you thought: a joyful raga must be full of happy words.
what it means: Bilaval opens with a singer admitting his words are too small, and singing anyway, gladly.
what a scholar hears: Guru Nanak's first Bilaval hymn (ang 795) turns on the court titles sultan and mian; the joy is in praising the One whose limit can't be known.
